ruleIntents.intent: Checks that every element in the document's sequential focus order produces some visible focus indication: when the element receives keyboard focus, at least one device pixel inside the visible viewport changes its HSL color value compared to the unfocused state. It is a pure pixel-diff (focused-vs-unfocused render) test — it does not care WHAT indicator appears (outline, border, injected square, background change), where it is, how large it is, or whether it is unique; only that SOME pixel differs. The canonical fail is CSS that strips the indicator (e.g. :focus { outline: none } with no replacement).
ruleIntents.scLimb: SC 2.4.7 Focus Visible: the single requirement that "any keyboard operable user interface has a mode of operation where the keyboard focus indicator is visible." This rule exercises the existence/visibility-of-the-focus-indicator limb — i.e. that a focus indicator is rendered (a perceptible visual change) for each focusable item. It deliberately does NOT exercise adjacent concerns owned by WCAG 2.2 (2.4.11 Focus Appearance size/contrast, 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured), which the rule text explicitly carves out and notes can still pass here while being problematic.
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to any element that is part of sequential focus navigation in an HTML document (i.e. in the tab/focus order: natively focusable elements like links and form controls, or elements made focusable via tabindex="0"). Excludes: documents with no focusable element (Inapplicable Example 1), and elements removed from the tab order via tabindex="-1" (Inapplicable Example 2). Required input aspects: CSS styling and the DOM tree — the rule must render the page to diff pixels.
ruleIntents.expectation: For each in-scope target element, there is at least one device pixel inside the scrolling area of the viewport whose HSL color value differs between the focused and unfocused states. Pass = at least one pixel changes on focus (anywhere in viewport, any magnitude); Fail = zero pixels change on focus. Outcome mapping: any failed outcome means SC 2.4.7 is not satisfied; all-passed or inapplicable means the SC needs further (manual) testing — passing this rule is necessary but not sufficient for conformance.
scenarioTypesPresent: Default UA focus outline on a native link (bare <a href>) — Passed Example 1 and the provided passed fixture
Default UA focus outline on a scripted-focusable element (<span tabindex="0">) — Passed Example 2
Focus indicator on an ancestor rather than the element itself (parent <span> draws a border on focus via JS class toggle) — Passed Example 3
Focus indicator that is a separate adjacent element / injected visual (blue square shown next to the link), across multiple chained focusable elements — Passed Example 4
Focus indicator deliberately removed by author CSS (:focus { outline:none } with no replacement) → zero pixel change — Failed Example 1 and the provided failed fixture
No focusable element at all (plain <span>) — Inapplicable Example 1
Focusable elements explicitly pulled out of the tab order with tabindex="-1" — Inapplicable Example 2
syntheticNarrowness: Each fixture is a single bare element (one link) in an otherwise empty body — no real page chrome, layout, surrounding content, or competing focus styles; the diff is trivially isolated and never has to attribute a pixel change to the RIGHT element among many.

Only link/<a> and <span tabindex=0> are exercised; no buttons, inputs, selects, textareas, checkboxes, custom widgets (role=button), menu/tab/listbox composites, contenteditable, or summary/details — the broad real-world space of focusable controls is absent.

The fail case is the single most blatant pattern (outline:none with literally no replacement). Real-world 2.4.7 failures are subtler: indicator present but clipped by overflow:hidden, hidden behind a sticky header (overlaps 2.4.12), :focus styled but only :hover/:active intended, focus-visible vs focus mismatches, JS that moves focus then immediately blurs, or an indicator that changes layout but not color.

Pass cases include a 'pixel changes anywhere in the viewport' edge (Passed 3/4 use ancestor borders and detached squares) but the synthetic pages place those indicators immediately adjacent; they never test the rule's own admitted loophole — a barely-perceptible 1-pixel change at the far end of a long/scrolled page that technically passes but is useless to users.

All indicators are high-contrast navy-on-white or a strong default outline; there is no low-contrast / near-threshold focus styling, no semi-transparent overlay, no anti-aliasing edge case, and no dark-mode / system-color (Highlight) dependency — so the HSL-difference test is never stressed near its detection boundary.

Static, single-state JS at most (onfocus/onblur class toggle); no asynchronous focus changes, no animated/transitioned indicators, no focus indicators that depend on prefers-reduced-motion, and no SPA/dynamically-inserted focusable content — the rendered focused-vs-unfocused snapshot is always deterministic and immediate.

Tab order itself is trivial (one or three elements in source order); nothing tests reading-vs-focus-order, tabindex>0 reordering, or shadow DOM / iframe focus participation, so the 'part of sequential focus navigation' applicability is only ever the easy native case.

No viewport/scroll interplay in the provided fixtures: indicators are always on-screen, so the 'inside the scrolling area of the viewport' qualifier in the expectation is never actually tested against an off-screen or scrolled-out focus indicator.

contentDomainsPresent: Bare hyperlinks (<a href> to external sites: act-rules.github.io, w3.org) — the ONLY interactive content in the entire corpus
Generic span with tabindex=0 made focusable (Passed Example 2)
Links removed from sequential focus order via tabindex=-1 (Inapplicable Example 2)
Minimal bare HTML documents — no real page chrome, no forms, no widgets, no layout, no images
scLimbsCoveredByACT: Core intent: 'a person can know which element has the keyboard focus' — the rule's Expectation (>=1 device pixel inside the viewport changes HSL color when focused vs not) is a direct, testable proxy for the SC goal that a focus indicator be visible. Covered by all 9 cases.

Applicability limb: only elements 'in sequential focus navigation' (i.e. keyboard-operable, in tab order) are in scope. Covered positively (PE1 <a>, PE2 span tabindex=0) and negatively (IE1 no focusable element -> DNA; IE2 tabindex=-1 elements not in sequential focus order -> DNA). This matches the SC's 'Any keyboard operable user interface' scoping and the TT 'DNA if no elements can receive keyboard focus'.
Sufficient technique G149/G165 (user-agent default focus indicator): Passed Example 1 (<a>) and Passed Example 2 (span tabindex=0) rely on the browser's default outline.

Sufficient technique C15/SCR31 (author-supplied indicator via CSS/script change on focus): PE3 uses a CSS border on a parent span toggled on focus; PE4 uses JS onfocus/onblur toggling a navy background square (SCR31-style). G195 author-supplied indicator is represented.

Failure F78 limb (default outline removed via styling with no author replacement): Failed Example 1 sets `.no-focus-default:focus { outline: none }` and supplies no substitute — the single FAIL case, and the canonical F78 failure.
scLimbsAbsentFromACT: 'mode of operation where the focus indicator is visible' / multi-mode limb (Understanding Intent para + TT condition 'has a MODE of operation'): NO case exercises :focus-visible vs :focus, keyboard-vs-mouse-triggered indication, or any element that shows focus in one mode but not another. Sufficient technique C45 (:focus-visible) has zero test cases. The 'at least one mode' nuance is entirely untested.

'The focus indicator must not be time limited; when the keyboard focus is shown it must remain' (Understanding Intent, explicit sentence): NO case has a focus indicator that appears then disappears/times out while focus is retained. This temporal limb is completely absent.

Failure F55 limb (script removes focus when focus is received, e.g. onfocus=this.blur()): listed as a failure technique for 2.4.7 but has NO test case. The corpus has no script-driven focus-removal / focus-stealing failure.

Two-color / contrast-against-all-backgrounds limb (sufficient technique C40, and ACT Background note that a near-imperceptible change still technically passes): NO case tests a focus indicator with insufficient contrast against the background it overlaps, or an indicator visible on some backgrounds but not others. The 'barely perceptible change' edge the rule explicitly admits is not probed.

F78's other two failure sub-modes are absent: (a) author outline on the element that LOOKS like the focus indicator so you can't tell which element is focused; (b) a thick same-color border that occludes/hides the focus indicator even though the UA draws it. Only F78's 'outline:none' sub-mode is present.

Frame focus disambiguation limb (Trusted Tester 4.D step 2a + the entire frame Note): browsers may not show focus on a FRAME and that is explicitly NOT a failure. No <iframe>/<frame> case exists, so this exception is untested.

Form controls limb (Understanding Example 1: text field shows a caret/highlight on focus): NO <input>, <textarea>, <select>, <button>, checkbox or radio appears anywhere. The text-cursor/text-highlight focus indicator example from the Understanding doc is entirely absent.

Native interactive widgets beyond <a> and tabindex spans (buttons, custom ARIA widgets, menus, dialogs, tabs): none present, so 'all interactive interface components' (TT applicability list: drop-down menus, tooltips, revealing/hiding content) is untested.
varietyGaps: ELEMENT-TYPE monoculture: 8 of 9 cases use a bare <a href> link and the 9th a tabindex span. No native form controls (input/select/textarea/button), no custom/ARIA widgets, no composite components — the SC applies to 'any keyboard operable UI' but the corpus only proves links.

INDICATOR-MECHANISM gaps: covers UA default outline, parent-border-on-focus, and JS background-square. Missing: :focus-visible pseudo-class (C45), caret/text-highlight in a text field (Understanding Example 1), color-only change, box-shadow/ring indicators, and two-color indicators (C40).

FAILURE-MODE thinness: exactly 1 FAIL case, and it covers only ONE of the documented failures (F78 'outline:none'). Entirely missing: F55 (onfocus blur / script removes focus), F78 occluding-border and look-alike-outline sub-modes, time-limited/disappearing indicators, and indicators with too-low contrast to perceive.

OUTCOME imbalance: 5 passed / 1 failed / 3 inapplicable, and the inapplicable+duplicate cases inflate the count — IE2/PE4 each appear twice (WCAG21 vs WCAG22 URL variants), so effective distinct scenarios are ~6. Failures are severely underrepresented (~11%).

CONTENT-DOMAIN sterility: every page is a near-empty document containing one or two off-site links to act-rules.github.io / w3.org. No realistic page context — no navigation, forms, dialogs, data tables, multi-widget pages, or focus moving across many heterogeneous controls (the realistic 'tab through the whole page' scenario both TT 4.D and F78/F55 procedures describe).

TEMPORAL/MODE dimension wholly unrepresented: nothing dynamic over time (indicator that fades), nothing mode-dependent (keyboard vs pointer), and no frame/iframe — three explicit limbs of the SC/TT/Understanding text with zero coverage.

aspects.title: Focus indicator renders but is perceptually indistinguishable — resting style mimics the ring, or a thick same-color border swallows it (F78 modes 2 & 3)
aspects.description: F78 documents two failures where the focus indicator IS drawn (pixels change on focus) yet a sighted keyboard user still cannot tell which element is focused. Mode 2: the author gives every link/control a permanent static outline that looks identical to the browser focus ring (e.g. a {outline: thin dotted black}); when one element focuses, the UA overlays its own dotted ring, but because all elements already look dotted/outlined, the focused one is not distinguishable from its neighbours. Mode 3: the element has a thick border in the same color as the focus ring (e.g. a {border: medium solid black}); the UA draws its black ring just outside the border, but as both are black and the border is thicker, the ring 'no longer meets the definition of visible' against it. In both, the pixel diff is non-zero so the rule passes, yet the SC purpose — 'help a person know which element has the keyboard focus' — is defeated. Catching this requires a human to compare the focused appearance against the resting appearance of ALL elements (mode 2) or against the adjacent colors (mode 3) and judge whether the difference is genuinely distinguishing, not merely non-zero.
aspects.scLimb: The distinguishability/perceptibility limb of 'the keyboard focus indicator is visible': an indicator must let the user know WHICH element has focus, not merely cause some pixel to change. F78 explicitly carves out these 'present but not visible' cases as failures of 2.4.7.
aspects.whyUncovered: oj04fd is a pure focused-vs-unfocused pixel diff on a SINGLE element that 'does not care how large it is' or whether it is perceptible, and it never compares the focused element against the resting look of OTHER elements or against its own adjacent colors. The ACT fail fixture is only the blatant outline:none case; there is no fixture pairing a focus-ring-mimicking resting outline or a thick same-color border with the default ring. A fully-automated tool registers the non-zero edge-pixel diff and passes; only human visual judgment about distinguishability/perceptual contrast against context can catch it.

references.quote: The following CSS example will create an outline around links that looks the same as the focus indicator. This makes it impossible for users to determine which one in fact has the focus, even though the user agent does draw the focus indicator.
the focus indicator is drawn just outside the border, but as both are black and the border is thicker than the focus indicator, it no longer meets the definition of "visible".
The purpose of this success criterion is to help a person know which element has the keyboard focus.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained pages where the focused state produces a real but non-distinguishing pixel diff. For mode 2, give every focusable element a permanent outline/border whose style, weight and color match the UA focus ring so the focused element blends into siblings. For mode 3, give the element a thick border in the exact color of the ring so the added ring is absorbed. Use a variety of control types (links, buttons, inputs) to broaden beyond the ACT corpus's link-only fixtures. Do NOT strip the UA outline — the point is that pixels DO change but the change is camouflaged.
suggestedScenarios: A horizontal nav bar of 6 links each given a permanent 'outline: 1px dotted #000'; on focus the UA dotted ring is added, so the focused link looks essentially identical to its five neighbours.

A form where every input has resting 'outline: 2px solid #0000ff' and :focus yields a blue outline of similar weight, so tabbing produces no perceptible change to a human despite a small edge-pixel diff.
A set of links each with 'border: 4px solid black' on a white page; the 1px black UA focus ring drawn outside the border is visually absorbed by the thick black frame.
A toolbar of buttons each with a permanent 5px dark border identical in hue to the navy focus ring, so the focused button's added ring is buried in its own resting border.
A card grid where each focusable card has a static 1px dotted outline and the focused card gains a 1px dotted UA outline just outside, doubling the line but reading as the same decorative frame.
A vertical menu where author CSS gives every item a faint dotted underline matching the focus indicator style, so the ring on the active item is camouflaged among identical-looking siblings.

aspects.title: Focus indicator present but near the perception threshold — too thin, too low-contrast, or too small to be genuinely seen
aspects.description: An indicator can satisfy the pixel-diff rule while remaining effectively invisible to a human. G195 sets concrete guidance for a genuinely visible author indicator: an area at least a 1 CSS px border around the component (or at least 4 CSS px along the shortest side), and a contrast change of 3:1 or more between focused and unfocused states (or, failing 3:1, at least 2px thick). A page can change SOME pixels with a 1px outline whose color barely differs from the background, a faint sub-3:1 box-shadow, or a fractional letter-spacing nudge that only shifts a few antialiased edge pixels — so the diff is non-zero but no human can reliably perceive the focus. The SC's own purpose ('help a person know which element has focus', 'without a focus indicator sighted keyboard users cannot operate the page') implies the change must actually be noticeable; deciding whether a given magnitude/contrast/size crosses the perceptible line is a visual judgment, distinct from camouflage-against-neighbours.
aspects.scLimb: The 'is the indicator actually visible' magnitude limb — the SC's admitted loophole that ANY pixel change passes oj04fd even when the change is below human perceptibility. This sits within 2.4.7's purpose rather than borrowing the precise 2.4.11/2.4.13 numbers; G195 is the technique that articulates the threshold.
aspects.whyUncovered: oj04fd 'does not care WHAT indicator appears... how large it is' and passes on ANY magnitude of HSL change; the corpus uses only high-contrast navy-on-white or strong default outlines and never stresses the HSL-difference test near its detection boundary. There is no near-threshold fixture. A fully-automated 'did a pixel change' checker cannot decide whether a ~1px, ~1.2:1 indicator is noticeable to a human eye in context — that is exactly the human visual judgment the SC purpose requires.

references.quote: Check that the focus indicator area is at least the size of a 1 CSS px border around the component.
Check that the change of contrast of the indicator between focused and unfocused states has a ratio of 3:1 or more for the minimum focus indicator area.
Without a focus indicator, sighted keyboard users cannot operate the page.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages whose :focus produces a deliberately sub-perceptual change: tiny HSL color shifts on the indicator, ultra-thin/blurred shadows well under 3:1, or geometry nudges that move only a handful of antialiased pixels. Each must be a genuine, real pixel change (so oj04fd passes) but plausibly invisible to a human at normal viewing. Vary the control type and the indicator mechanism (color, shadow, outline width, spacing) so the set probes different facets of the threshold rather than one knob.
suggestedScenarios: A link whose :focus shifts text color from #000000 to #0a0a0a on white — a real but sub-perceptual HSL change that passes a pixel diff yet is invisible to a human.
A button with ':focus { outline: 1px solid #f4f4f4 }' on a #ffffff page: the indicator exists but its contrast with the background is far below noticeable.
An input whose only focus change is a 1px-wide light-grey box-shadow blurred to near-invisibility (well under 3:1 and under the 4px shortest-side area).
A small 8px-square custom checkbox whose focus indicator is a single off-white pixel-thin highlight on one edge — changed but below the 4 CSS px shortest-side guidance.
A link whose focus only nudges letter-spacing by a fraction, shifting a handful of antialiased edge pixels: a non-zero diff with no humanly perceptible focus cue.
A select whose :focus changes the background from #ffffff to #fdfdfd, a technically-different but visually-identical state.

aspects.title: Script removes or steals focus the instant an element receives it (F55: onfocus blur / programmatic focus theft)
aspects.description: F55 is a failure where script removes focus the moment an element receives it (onfocus="this.blur()", or a handler that immediately moves focus elsewhere). Because focus never settles, no focus indicator is ever shown for that element, and the control becomes pointer-only. This is a temporal/behavioral failure: a single focused snapshot may even render as unfocused because focus has already been stolen. F55's test requires confirming that 'when focus is placed on each element, focus remains there until user moves it' — a property over time, not a single render. The brief notes the corpus is static, single-state, with no asynchronous focus changes and no JS that moves focus then immediately blurs.
aspects.scLimb: The 'focus must remain / be shown when received' temporal limb: the Understanding text states the focus indicator must not be time-limited — 'when the keyboard focus is shown it must remain.' F55 lists 2.4.7 among the SCs it fails. Catching it requires reasoning about the script's effect on focus over time.
aspects.whyUncovered: oj04fd diffs a single focused snapshot vs an unfocused snapshot of an element it has programmatically focused; if a script blurs immediately, the rule's own focus attempt fails to settle, putting the case outside its clean pass/fail model, and no ACT fixture exercises blur-on-focus. A static pixel-diff cannot model 'focus is removed when received'; F55 explicitly requires a temporal/behavioral check (focus remains until the user moves it) that needs human or dynamic testing.

references.quote: Content that normally receives focus when the content is accessed by keyboard may have this focus removed by scripting. This is sometimes done when designer considers the system focus indicator to be unsightly.
Check that when focus is placed on each element, focus remains there until user moves it.
The focus indicator must not be time limited, when the keyboard focus is shown it must remain.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages with focusable controls whose focus is removed or relocated by script the instant it lands. Use the canonical F55 patterns (onfocus blur, focusin handler that moves focus) across different control types. The test must drive keyboard focus (Tab) and observe over time that the indicator never persists on the intended element — a static single snapshot is insufficient, so scenarios should make the focus theft happen via real event handlers.
suggestedScenarios: A submit button with onfocus="this.blur()" so tabbing to it instantly loses focus and no indicator ever appears.
A link <a href onfocus="if(this.blur)this.blur();"> that drops focus the moment Tab reaches it.
An image link where keyboard users get no focus state at all.
A custom widget (role=button, tabindex=0) whose focusin handler calls document.body.focus(), bouncing focus off the control silently.
A search field that on focus immediately moves focus to a hidden element, so the visible control never shows a focus ring.
A set of nav links where a delegated focusin listener blurs the active element after a short timeout, so the indicator flashes then disappears before settling.

aspects.title: Visual feedback exists only for pointer interaction (:hover/:active) or is suppressed for keyboard (:focus-visible mismatch), leaving keyboard focus bare
aspects.description: C15 and C45 stress that the visible feedback must apply to the KEYBOARD focus state, not only pointer interaction. A common real-world failure: authors write ':hover {…}' and ':active {…}' (or rely on JS mouseenter/mouseleave) but never ':focus'/':focus-visible', while also stripping the UA outline. A mouse user sees rich feedback; a keyboard user tabbing through gets nothing. The subtle, judgment-requiring variants are where this matters: :focus-visible heuristics that the UA suppresses for certain elements, :focus reused for both states but styled with mouse-targeted changes, or focus-within applied to a non-focusable wrapper while the real target has outline:none. Distinguishing 'this feedback is pointer-only / modality-mismatched' from 'this is a real keyboard focus indicator' requires understanding the selectors' modality semantics — which input actually triggers the change a keyboard user receives.
aspects.scLimb: The 'mode of operation where the KEYBOARD focus indicator is visible' limb — the indicator must be present specifically for keyboard navigation, not just on pointer hover/active. C45 explains :focus-visible is shown for keyboard but generally not for pointer, making the modality distinction central.
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT corpus includes only :focus / UA-outline cases and the single outline:none fail; it has no fixture where feedback lives solely on :hover/:active or on a UA-suppressed :focus-visible path. A blatant hover-only-with-outline:none page would fail oj04fd (zero diff under programmatic focus), but the SUBTLE variants — :focus-visible suppressed for a given element type, mouse-driven JS toggles, or focus-within on the wrong node — require a human to reason about which modality actually drives the visible change; a pixel diff cannot attribute a change to input modality.

references.quote: browsers always show these styles when a user is navigating using the keyboard, but will generally not show them as a result of a mouse/pointer interaction
Providing visual feedback may be possible through more than one mode. Usually, it is attained through using a mouse to hover over the element or a keyboard to tab to the element.
Ensure each item receiving focus has a visible indicator.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages where the only styled state is pointer-driven or modality-mismatched, with the UA outline stripped. Include the obvious case (:hover/:active only) but emphasize the subtle ones: JS mouseenter/mouseleave toggles instead of focus events, :focus-within on a non-focusable wrapper, and :focus styling whose visible effect a keyboard user does not actually receive. The test should drive keyboard focus (not mouse) and judge whether a real indicator appears for the keyboard user.
suggestedScenarios: Nav links with ':focus { outline: none }' plus ':hover { background: #dcffff }' — mouse users see a highlight, keyboard users see nothing.
Buttons that only define ':active { transform: scale(0.98) }' and suppress the focus outline, so Tab produces no visible state.
Inputs with a rich ':hover' border-color change but a stripped ':focus', so tabbing through the form gives no focus cue.
A card list where ':focus-within' is applied to a non-focusable wrapper while the real link has outline:none, leaving keyboard focus invisible on the actual target.
A widget that styles ':hover' and ':focus' identically but triggers the highlight via mouseenter/mouseleave JS rather than focus events, so keyboard focus never activates it.
A menu where items light up only on a JS mousemove handler and the UA outline is removed, so arrow-key/Tab navigation shows no focused item.

aspects.title: Custom-drawn indicator that vanishes in forced-colors mode or that AT cannot track (G165 / C40 caveats)
aspects.description: G165 warns that if you draw your OWN focus indicator (e.g. coloring sections of the page in response to user action) rather than using the native indicator, user/AT system-wide focus customizations 'will not carry over, and AT will not usually be able to find your focus indicator.' C40 adds the forced-colors caveat: relying on box-shadow alone fails because 'user agents commonly suppress the box-shadow property in forced-color modes.' So an indicator can look fine in the single default render oj04fd snapshots, yet disappear (box-shadow / background-image / gradient suppressed) or become orphaned from the real focus position (detached painted square, overlay) for users in Windows High Contrast / forced-colors mode or for AT users relying on the native ring. Judging whether the chosen technique is robust across forced colors and tracks the actual focus is a semantic/contextual judgment about the indicator mechanism, not a default-mode pixel count.
aspects.scLimb: The robustness / 'mode of operation' limb under real user rendering conditions — the Understanding text frames 2.4.7 as ensuring at least one mode where focus is visible; G165/C40 show that a default-render-only indicator can fail to be that mode for forced-colors and AT users.
aspects.whyUncovered: oj04fd renders one default-mode snapshot and accepts a box-shadow-only, gradient, or JS-painted indicator as a pass because pixels change; it does not simulate forced-colors mode and the corpus has no dark-mode / system-color (Highlight) dependency. The corpus's Passed Examples 3/4 even use the exact 'drawn, detached' indicators G165 warns about, but never test them under forced colors or for focus-tracking robustness. Recognizing that a box-shadow-only / background-image / JS-painted indicator will be suppressed or orphaned for these users requires a human (or a deliberate forced-colors/AT mode toggle) — a default-render checker cannot.

references.quote: If you draw your own focus indicator, for example by coloring sections of the page in response to user action, these settings will not carry over, and AT will not usually be able to find your focus indicator.
User agents commonly suppress the box-shadow property in forced-color modes, so authors should avoid relying on box-shadow alone to implement focus indicators.
If you use the native focus indicator, any system-wide settings for its visibility will carry over to the web page.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages whose ONLY focus indicator is implemented via a mechanism that forced-colors mode suppresses (box-shadow alone, background-image, CSS gradient swap) or via a JS-painted/detached marker that is orphaned from the real focus position. Each must look fine in the default render (so oj04fd passes) but fail when the indicator mechanism is suppressed or when AT seeks the native ring. The test should consider forced-colors / high-contrast rendering and whether the cue tracks the actual focused element, not just the default snapshot.
suggestedScenarios: A button whose only focus indicator is ':focus { outline: none; box-shadow: 0 0 0 3px blue }' — visible normally but suppressed in forced-colors mode, leaving no indicator.
Links where focus paints a detached colored square via JS far from the link; in forced-colors mode or for AT users the square is orphaned from the actual focus position.
A page where ':focus' sets only 'background-image: url(focus-ring.svg)'; background images are dropped in forced-colors mode, removing the cue.
A control with outline:none plus a semi-transparent overlay element as its focus marker; the overlay is invisible against the system Highlight color in high-contrast mode.
A nav whose focus indicator is a CSS gradient background swap that forced-colors mode flattens, eliminating the perceptible difference.
A custom listbox that highlights the active option by recoloring a sibling div via JS rather than moving native focus, so AT/forced-colors users get no trackable indicator.

aspects.title: Focus indicator drawn but clipped by overflow or pushed outside the visible viewport so the user never sees it
aspects.description: The SC requires a perceptible focus indication for the focused element. A real-world failure: the element receives focus and an indicator IS drawn, but it is clipped by an ancestor's overflow:hidden, hidden behind a sticky/fixed header or off-canvas panel, or the focused element sits scrolled out of the visible viewport, so the changed pixels are never actually seen by the user. Because oj04fd counts a pixel change 'inside the scrolling area of the viewport' and never requires the user to be able to see it without manual scrolling — and the corpus places every indicator immediately adjacent in an otherwise empty body — these clipping/scroll cases are untested. Whether the indicator is actually visible to the user (vs technically painted but clipped/offscreen) is a layout/perception judgment; note this partially overlaps WCAG 2.2's 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured, but the bare 'I cannot see any focus indicator at all' outcome still implicates 2.4.7.
aspects.scLimb: The 'the indicator is actually visible to the user' limb — the indicator must be perceivable in the viewport, not merely rendered somewhere in the layout. Overlaps 2.4.12/2.4.11 (Focus Not Obscured) at the edge, but a fully-clipped/offscreen indicator means no visible focus at all, squarely 2.4.7.
aspects.whyUncovered: oj04fd accepts ANY changed pixel anywhere in the scrolling area and the corpus's single bare element in an empty body never has to deal with clipping containers, sticky overlays, or scroll position; there is no fixture where the indicator is painted but clipped/offscreen. A pixel-diff that scans the whole render surface (or auto-scrolls the element into view) reports a change and passes; judging whether a real user navigating by keyboard would actually SEE the indicator given overflow/sticky/scroll context is a layout-aware human visual judgment.

references.quote: Why it's important: Without a focus indicator, sighted keyboard users cannot operate the page.
Ensure each item receiving focus has a visible indicator.

It can be difficult to see the line when it is around a form element which already has an outline, when the focused element is inside a table cell, when the focused element is very small, or when the background of the page is a dark color.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages where a focusable element's indicator is drawn but not visible to the user: place the control inside an overflow:hidden container that clips the ring, behind a position:sticky/fixed header that overlaps the focused row, or far enough down a tall scroll container that the focused element (and its ring) is outside the initial viewport. The test should drive keyboard Tab and judge from the user's actual viewport whether any focus cue is perceivable, rather than scanning the full render surface.
suggestedScenarios: A scrollable card with overflow:hidden where a focusable child's outline is clipped at the container edge so the ring is never fully visible.
A long page with a tall position:sticky header; tabbing to a link near the top scrolls it under the header, hiding the focus ring behind the sticky bar.
A horizontally-scrolling toolbar with overflow:hidden where the focused button's right-side outline is clipped off the visible track.
A modal-like panel with overflow:hidden and rounded corners that clip the focus outline of the first/last focusable control.

pages.scenario: Farm-to-table bistro primary navigation. Links light up with a pale-mint pill (#dcffff) on :hover/:active; the UA focus ring is removed via nav.primary a:focus{outline:none} with no replacement. A mouse user sees the pill; a keyboard user tabbing through the menu sees nothing change on the focused link. HEAD case (website-builder/marketing-template default).
pages.mechanism: Visible feedback is bound exclusively to pointer-modality pseudo-classes (:hover and :active). Tab fires :focus, whose only declared rule is outline:none, so the keyboard-focused link is pixel-identical to its idle state. The link is still announced to screen readers, but the sighted keyboard user — the population 2.4.7 protects — has no indication of focus position.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: outline:none is legal CSS and a valid focus indicator could plausibly live on :hover/:focus/box-shadow/a class; there is no reliable automated oracle for SC 2.4.7. A scanner cannot reason that the only state carrying a perceptible change (:hover) is pointer-triggered and never responds to keyboard focus. Verified in Chromium: focusDelta=0 visual properties on every nav link.

citation.quote: Styles defined with the regular :focus pseudo-class are applied whenever an element has focus, regardless of how it received focus. In contrast, user agents apply additional heuristics and logic to decide when to show :focus-visible styles – in particular, browsers always show these styles when a user is navigating using the keyboard, but will generally not show them as a result of a mouse/pointer interaction (with the exception of elements that also support keyboard input, such as <input> elements).

pages.scenario: Real-estate listings card grid. Each card (<article>) has a lift+shadow bound to .card:hover and .card:focus-within; the real focusable address <a> has outline:none. Tabbing onto a listing DOES lift the wrapper card, but the lift is on the wrong node, is pixel-identical to hover, and the focused link itself is bare. LONG-TAIL case (designer wired the interaction to the whole tile).
pages.mechanism: Subtle present-but-wrong-node failure. On Tab, :focus-within fires and the wrapper lifts (transform:translateY(-3px) + shadow), so something visibly changes — but it marks the entire tile rather than the focused control (the link's own outline was removed), so with multiple cards visible the user cannot tell which element holds focus, and the change is indistinguishable from hover. A naive 'did anything change under programmatic focus?' pixel-diff (like oj04fd) would be fooled into passing.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Because a perceptible change occurs on focus, any heuristic that only asks whether the page looks different under programmatic focus passes — including diff-based checks. Judging that the change is on the wrong node, is identical to hover, and leaves the real target bare requires human reasoning about which element focus is on versus where the feedback appears. Verified in Chromium: wrapper transform none -> matrix(1,0,0,1,0,-3) and shadow appear on keyboard focus, yet the focused link's outline stays none.

pages.scenario: E-commerce checkout shipping-country field built as an ARIA combobox with aria-activedescendant. The blue option highlight (.opt.hot) is toggled only by mousemove/mouseleave; the ArrowUp/ArrowDown handler updates aria-activedescendant (so screen readers announce the active country) but never paints the active option, and no CSS targets the active descendant. A sighted keyboard user arrowing the list sees nothing move. LONG-TAIL case (mouse-era autocomplete ported to ARIA).
pages.mechanism: In an aria-activedescendant widget DOM focus stays on the input, so the visually-indicated active option IS the focus indicator the keyboard user needs. Here the highlight (.opt.hot) is bound to mousemove, a pointer event keyboard navigation cannot fire; the keydown handler moves aria-activedescendant but applies no class, and there is no [aria-activedescendant]-correlated CSS rule. The screen-reader user hears the active option; the sighted keyboard user sees the highlight frozen on whatever the mouse last touched, or nothing.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The ARIA plumbing is textbook-correct (valid roles, accessible name via aria-labelledby, aria-activedescendant references a real option and updates on arrow keys) — axe actively rewards this. No scanner correlates 'the keyboard moves the active descendant' with 'no CSS ever makes that descendant look different' because the highlight is gated behind pointer-only JS. Verified in Chromium: two ArrowDown presses moved aria-activedescendant to opt-it (Italy) with zero options highlighted; a pointer mousemove over Spain painted opt-es rgb(37,99,235).

pages.scenario: SaaS pricing page (Solo/Team/Business) with one CTA <button> per tier. The buttons define exactly one styled interactive state: .cta:active{transform:scale(.97)} (a press animation); .cta:focus is reset to outline:none with no replacement. pages.mechanism: :active is the 'currently being activated' state, not a focus state. It fires for a mouse press and for keyboard Space/Enter activation but lasts only while the control is held and reverts instantly on release. With :focus reset to outline:none and no persistent replacement, a keyboard user who Tabs to a CTA and stops sees the button exactly as idle and cannot tell which of the three CTAs holds focus — violating the requirement that the indicator remain while focus is shown.

Distinguishing transient, modality-agnostic press feedback (:active) from persistent focus feedback (:focus/:focus-visible) is a semantic judgment about which state a Tab-and-stop produces. Mechanism depends on a fixed 1280px viewport: at the authored width the card right edge is x=999 and the ring overhangs to x=1018. At narrower widths the card shrinks but the translateX(13px) overhang is constant, so the clip relationship holds — verified non-fragile, but worth noting the geometry is width-anchored.

TASK-PROMPT MISMATCH (not a page defect, but flagged per instructions): the prompt's claimed scenario/mechanism/selector describe a DIFFERENT case than this file. Prompt claims a 'long-form news article with an in-article TOC', a position:sticky masthead (~135px), :target fragment navigation, selector '#policy:target', and mechanism 'targetTop=0 while stickyBottom=135, headingHiddenUnderSticky=true'. NONE of this is on the page: probe shows policyExists=false; .gov-bar is explicitly 'NOT sticky — ordinary document flow' (case-02.html L14-15); there is no TOC, no :target rule, no fragment navigation. The page's ACTUAL mechanism is focus({preventScroll:true}) on a below-fold field. The reviewer must judge the page on its own HTML+MD, which are internally consistent.

The selector supplied in the task prompt (#policy:target) does not exist in the file; the real element under test is #email (confirmed policyExists=false via probe). Verdict was assessed against the actual page content.

Minor citation-fit nuance (not a defect): the F78 quoted sentence lists examples about color/border SIMILARITY ('outlines that look the same as the focus outline', 'thick borders... same color as the focus indicator'), whereas this failure is geometric CLIPPING by overflow:hidden. The quote is verbatim (F78.html lines 29-31) and F78's broader description (line 27: indicator 'rendered non-visible by other styling on the page') fairly covers clip-based removal, so the citation is defensible but not a precise match to the listed examples.

Cosmetic: the inspect tool's `.tool:focus-visible` selector resolved to the 3rd button (U̲ تسطير, x=742) rather than the first; the geometry that proves the failure had to be measured with a direct Tab+boundingRect probe (first button focused: x=935→right=1023 vs toolbar clip right=981). This is a tool quirk, not a page defect.

Citation application is at the edge of F78's literal scope: F78's body and three examples address indicators that are turned off (outline:none), confusable with other outlines, or occluded by same-color borders — not clipping by an ancestor overflow/contain box. The quoted sentence DOES cover 'rendered non-visible by other styling,' and the partial clip of the ring's left/bottom rails + rounded corner is a reasonable application, but it is a borderline (partial-clip, not full-removal) reading rather than a textbook F78 example. This is acceptable for a human-judgment corpus but worth noting.

contain:paint is not strictly load-bearing for the failure — overflow:hidden alone fully accounts for the clip. The doc presents the two as stacked clip mechanisms (true), but a reader could over-credit contain:paint; the failure persists with overflow:hidden alone.

Selector under test '#cvc:focus-visible' is not statically matchable: the inspect.js querySelector returns 'selector not found' because :focus-visible only matches a keyboard-focused element. Not a page defect, but the selector cannot be resolved without live focus; live Puppeteer tabbing was required to confirm.

Minor naming nit: the case is labeled errorIsReal=false because it is a deliberate true-negative/PASS boundary variant (no accessibility error exists, by design); the 'passed' outcome label is the thing being verified and it is correct.
